prompt: The web shop sends a new export every month. What does importing it through Power Query keep that opening it with a double-click does not?
hint: Think about next month, not this one.

choices.text: The fixes, as a list of steps that runs again on the next file
choices.why: Right. Applied Steps is the recipe, and Refresh All replays it on whatever the source holds now.

choices.text: A copy of every month's file, stored inside the workbook
choices.why: Power Query reads the file where it is; it keeps no copy of the source, only the result it loads.

choices.text: A macro recorded from the clicks you made
choices.why: No code runs in the workbook and no clicks are recorded. Each step says what to do to the data.

choices.text: A formula that recalculates by itself whenever the file is saved
choices.why: A query runs when it is refreshed, not when its source changes.

prompt: You have refreshed a query a hundred times. What has happened to the CSV file it reads?
hint: Which direction does the data travel?

choices.text: It now holds the cleaned rows the query produced
choices.why: The cleaned rows live in the query's own table. Power Query reads its source and writes only to its result.

choices.text: Excel has converted it to .xlsx to read it faster
choices.why: The file stays a CSV in its folder; nothing renames or converts it.

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: Right. Power Query never writes to its source: the file is byte for byte the one you saved.

choices.text: Its cancelled orders have been removed by the filter step
choices.why: A filter step removes rows from the query's result, never from the file.

prompt: The courier's file in your folder is replaced by a corrected copy. When does the `Freight` table on your sheet show the correction?
hint: A query is not a formula.

choices.text: At once, as a cell formula would
choices.why: That is the difference the lesson draws: a formula recalculates when what it reads changes, and a query does not.

choices.text: The next time the workbook is saved
choices.why: Saving the workbook does not run its queries.

choices.text: Never, because a query reads its file only once, when it is created
choices.why: A query reads its source on every refresh; that is what makes it a recipe.

choices.text: At the next refresh, and not before
choices.why: Right. Between refreshes the table sits still, whatever happens to the file.

prompt: How were the numbers that lesson 13's import steps produce worked out?
hint: The lesson says it in its first section.

choices.text: By running the queries in Excel for Windows
choices.why: The course was written on a computer with no Excel, and says so.

choices.text: By a script that applies the same steps to the same files
choices.why: Right. Nothing in lessons 13 and 14 was run in Excel, and the lesson says so plainly.

choices.text: By LibreOffice Calc, which has its own Power Query
choices.why: Calc has no Power Query. It ran the formulas of lessons 1 to 12.

choices.text: By estimating from the size of each file
choices.why: Every number was computed from the files the lesson prints.

prompt: Why does the lesson choose **Do not detect data types** in the preview of a CSV file?
hint: Whose rules does a guess use?

choices.text: Detection is too slow to use on a file of more than a few rows
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given. The problem is which conventions a guessed type is read with.

choices.text: Detected types cannot be changed afterwards
choices.why: They can, but by then a date may already have been read in the wrong order.

choices.text: A guess uses your computer's rules, not the file's
choices.why: Right. Setting each type yourself, with the file's locale, gives the same answer on every computer.

choices.text: Power Query only detects types for files with a .txt extension
choices.why: Detection works on CSV files too; the lesson turns it off on purpose.

prompt: With its three columns typed using Portuguese (Brazil), what does the `Freight` column of `freight-2026-q3.csv` add up to, in reais?
hint: Twenty rows, read with a decimal comma.

prompt: You built the web query with **Using Locale…** and English (United States). A colleague whose Excel uses a decimal comma refreshes it. What does `45.00` become on their computer?
hint: Where is the locale written?

choices.text: 45, the same as on yours
choices.why: Right. The step carries "en-US", and that is the point of naming the locale: the answer no longer depends on who refreshes.

choices.text: 4500, because their computer reads the full stop as a thousands separator
choices.why: That is what a guessed type would do. The locale is written into the step, so their computer's rules are not asked.

choices.text: An error, because the two locales disagree
choices.why: Nothing disagrees: the step says how to read the text, and the text follows those rules.

choices.text: 45 only if their Windows is also set to English
choices.why: The step decides, not their Windows settings.

prompt: Match each text from the two files, read with the locale named, to what it becomes.
hint: One locale reads the full stop as a decimal mark, the other the comma.

prompt: Read with the wrong locale, the courier's file gives 10 errors and 8 silently wrong dates. Why does the lesson call the errors the lucky ones?
hint: Which of the two would you notice?

choices.text: Errors are removed automatically when the table loads
choices.why: An error arrives as an empty cell; nothing fixes it, it only stops being visible as text.

choices.text: Errors are counted in the freight total and make it obviously wrong
choices.why: The errors are in the date column, and a date does not enter the freight total.

choices.text: The wrong dates all fall on weekends and are easy to spot
choices.why: They are ordinary valid dates; nothing about them stands out.

choices.text: You see an error, while a wrong date looks like every other date
choices.why: Right. A shipment moved from July to March raises nothing, and only a strange monthly total would give it away.

prompt: In `Table.TransformColumnTypes(…, "pt-BR")`, the last argument names the ___ the text was written in: its conventions for decimals and dates.
hint: The dialog is called Using …

prompt: How many rows does `WebOrders` hold once the three files in `web` are combined?
hint: Each file's header line is used once, for the column names.

prompt: One month the platform starts writing a line of text above the header. Where does the step that skips it belong?
hint: Does every file need it on its own, or all the rows together?

choices.text: In `WebOrders`, after the files have been stacked
choices.why: By then the extra lines sit among the data rows of every month, and the header has already been read from the wrong line.

choices.text: In **Transform Sample File**
choices.why: Right. Steps there happen to each file before stacking, and a line above the header is a property of each file.

choices.text: In the monthly file, deleting the line by hand
choices.why: That works once and has to be done every month, which is the afternoon Power Query exists to remove.

choices.text: In the **Source** step of `WebOrders`, by filtering the `Name` column
choices.why: Filtering `Name` chooses which files are read, not which lines inside them.

prompt: Why does the lesson save the courier's invoice in `cafe-serra` rather than in `web`?
hint: What does From Folder do to every file it finds?

choices.text: Power Query cannot read two CSV files that sit in one folder
choices.why: It reads every file in the folder; that is exactly the danger.

choices.text: The invoice is quarterly, while the exports arrive every month
choices.why: The frequency does not matter to From Folder. The shape does.

choices.text: Excel locks a folder while one of its files is open
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson depends on locking; the issue is the file's shape.

choices.text: Every file in `web` gets the same steps, the invoice too
choices.why: Right. A folder query assumes every file has the same shape, and the filter on `Name` is the guard against one that does not.

prompt: October's export arrives. What do you do so that `WebOrders` includes it?
hint: Nothing in the query changes.

choices.text: Save it in `web` and choose **Data › Refresh All**
choices.why: Right. The query lists the folder again, finds four files and combines them all.

choices.text: Make a new query for it and append it to `WebOrders`
choices.why: That is the monthly work From Folder removes: the folder query already reads every file.

choices.text: Edit the `Source` step so its path names the new file
choices.why: The folder query names the folder, not a file, so there is nothing to edit.

choices.text: Paste its rows under the `WebOrders` table on the sheet
choices.why: Rows typed or pasted into a loaded table are overwritten at the next refresh.

prompt: What does the `Source.Name` column of `WebOrders` hold?
hint: It is the first column, and From Folder adds it.

choices.text: The name of the customer who placed the order
choices.why: The exports carry no customer column at all.

choices.text: The name of the file each row came from
choices.why: Right: `web-2026-07.csv` on the July rows, and so on. It tells the months apart even if a date were missing.

choices.text: The path of the folder, the same on every row
choices.why: The folder is the same for all; this column tells the files apart.

choices.text: The name of the query, `WebOrders`, on every row
choices.why: The query's name is not repeated on its rows.

prompt: Why is the `Sales` query, read with **From Table/Range**, closed with **Only Create Connection**?
hint: What would loading it to a sheet produce?

choices.text: A connection refreshes faster than a table
choices.why: Speed is not the argument. The problem is what a loaded copy would be.

choices.text: A query read from a table cannot be loaded onto any sheet at all
choices.why: It can; it would just duplicate what is already there.

choices.text: It would duplicate `Sales` on a sheet, to be kept in step
choices.why: Right. The table already exists; the query only needs to be available to other queries.

choices.text: Connections are the only queries lesson 14 can merge
choices.why: A merge works on any query; the choice is about not duplicating `Sales`.

prompt: A sale is added under the last row of the `Sales` table. What does the query read at the next refresh?
hint: Look at what its `Source` step names.

choices.text: 109 rows, because the step names the table and the table grew
choices.why: Right. `Excel.CurrentWorkbook(){[Name="Sales"]}` follows the table wherever its edge moves.

choices.text: 108 rows, because the query remembers the range it was built on
choices.why: That is what a fixed range would do; the step names a table, not cells.

choices.text: An error, because the table's size changed
choices.why: Growing is what a table is for; nothing breaks.

choices.text: 110 rows, the header included
choices.why: The table's header becomes the column names, not a row.

prompt: A colleague corrects a price in the workbook your query reads, and leaves the file open without saving. You refresh. What do you get?
hint: What does a query on another workbook read?

choices.text: The corrected price, because the file is open on the network
choices.why: Being open does not matter; the query reads the file on disk.

choices.text: An error, because the file is in use
choices.why: The lesson's warning is about what is read, not about a refusal.

choices.text: The old price, because only what was last saved is read
choices.why: Right. Until the correction is saved it exists only in their window, and "the refresh did not pick it up" is the usual surprise.

choices.text: The corrected price, but only after Excel asks your colleague
choices.why: Excel asks nobody; it reads the saved file.

prompt: You import a **sheet** of another workbook, not a table. Which of these happen? Choose all that apply.
hint: A sheet is every cell anybody used, and nothing marks its first row as a header.

choices.text: The header row arrives as data and needs a Promoted Headers step
choices.why: A sheet has no header of its own, so its first row is read as a row until a step promotes it.

choices.text: A note typed in J1 arrives as an extra, mostly empty column
choices.why: Every used cell comes with the sheet, and the query cannot tell a note from data.

choices.text: Only the cells inside the data's rectangle are read
choices.why: That is what a table gives you. A sheet brings everything on it.

choices.text: Changes typed into the open file and not yet saved are read
choices.why: The query reads the saved file, whatever kind of object it imports.

prompt: You connect to a database table of a million orders, filter `Date` to 2026 and remove four columns. With query folding, what reaches your computer?
hint: Who does the work of the steps?

choices.text: All million rows, which Excel then filters on your computer
choices.why: That is what happens with a file. With a database the steps become SQL and the server answers.

choices.text: A copy of the whole database, saved inside the workbook
choices.why: A query never copies its source; folding makes it read even less.

choices.text: The SQL text, which you then run by hand in the database
choices.why: Excel sends the SQL itself; **View Native Query** only lets you read it.

choices.text: Only 2026's rows, and only the columns you kept
choices.why: Right. The steps are translated into one SQL query and the server sends back its answer.

prompt: You send a colleague a workbook whose query reads a company database with your login. What happens when they refresh it?
hint: Where does Excel keep the answer to the credentials dialog?

choices.text: It refreshes with your login, which travels inside the workbook
choices.why: Credentials are kept on the computer that gave them, never inside the workbook.

choices.text: Excel asks them for credentials of their own
choices.why: Right. Your login stayed on your computer, so they need their own access to that server.

choices.text: The query is deleted, because it belongs to another user
choices.why: The query stays; only the credential is missing.

choices.text: It shows the rows from your last refresh and never asks
choices.why: A refresh reads the source again, which needs a login on their computer.

prompt: Right after `Source` you add a step that has no SQL equivalent, and then you filter `Date` to 2026. Where does the filter run?
hint: Folding stops at the first step the database does not understand.

choices.text: On the server, because a filter always folds there
choices.why: A filter folds only while everything before it has folded.

choices.text: On the server, after Excel sends it the step it did not understand
choices.why: Excel cannot send what has no SQL equivalent; that is why the folding stops.

choices.text: In Excel, on every row the server sent back
choices.why: Right. Once a step breaks the folding, every step after it runs in Excel, so filter early.

choices.text: Nowhere: the query refuses to run
choices.why: It runs; it just does more of the work itself.

prompt: Put the three ways a query on a web page breaks in order, from least to most dangerous.
hint: Danger here is how long it takes anybody to notice.
items: The page moves and the refresh fails
A column is renamed and a step cannot find it
A table is added above yours and the query reads the wrong one
trap: The quiet case is the worst one: a refresh with no error, on the wrong data.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer a CSV file published at an address to a table read off a web page?
hint: Who is each one made for?

choices.text: A page is rearranged at will; a file keeps its columns
choices.why: Right. A rearranged page can even refresh without an error on the wrong table.

choices.text: Power Query cannot read the tables inside an HTML page
choices.why: It can, through the Navigator; the lesson's worry is what happens later.

choices.text: A published file never changes once it is on the site
choices.why: It does change, with each release; what it tends to keep is its shape.

choices.text: Pages always need a login, and published files never do
choices.why: Public pages are read anonymously; the problem is their stability.

prompt: Excel asks you to set privacy levels when a query combines your own file with a public website. What is it protecting against?
hint: Think about what a filter can carry.

choices.text: Somebody on the website reading the workbook you saved
choices.why: A website cannot read your workbook; the risk runs the other way, through what the query sends.

choices.text: The website's data being saved permanently on your computer
choices.why: Downloading the data is what the query is for.

choices.text: Your refreshes slowing the website down for everybody else
choices.why: That is a database worry, the read-only copy of section 06.

choices.text: Your file's values being sent to the site, say in an address
choices.why: Right. Marking your files Private and the site Public keeps the two apart.

prompt: Match each destination in **Import Data** to the situation it suits.
hint: Who reads the result, and in what form?

pairs.right: A person needs to read or filter the rows
The rows are only ever read summarised
An intermediate query that others build on

pairs.left: Add this data to the Data Model
pairs.right: Tables to be related to each other, in lesson 15

right_distractors: Rows to be edited by hand every month

prompt: You type a corrected price into a cell of the loaded `WebOrders` table. What becomes of it?
hint: Who owns that table?

choices.text: It stays, and the query learns the correction from it
choices.why: A query does not read its own output; nothing learns from the typed value.

choices.text: It lasts until the next refresh writes over it
choices.why: Right. Fix the source file or add a step, and the fix survives every refresh.

choices.text: Excel refuses the edit, because a loaded table is locked
choices.why: Excel lets you type there, which is what makes the mistake easy.

choices.text: It is copied back into `web-2026-08.csv`
choices.why: Power Query never writes to its source.

prompt: Some dates failed to convert in a loaded query. Where does that show most clearly?
hint: What does an error look like once it reaches a sheet?

choices.text: As `#VALUE!` in every cell of the loaded table that failed
choices.why: A conversion error arrives in the table as an empty cell, which is why it is easy to miss.

choices.text: In a message box that appears at every refresh
choices.why: No box appears; the count in the pane is the signal.

choices.text: Nowhere at all, until some total looks wrong
choices.why: That is true of silently wrong dates, not of errors: the pane counts those.

choices.text: In the pane, under the query's name, as a count
choices.why: Right, and clicking it opens a query listing the rows that hold them.

prompt: Put the import of the courier's file in order.
hint: The types are set after the editor opens, and the name last.
items: Data › Get Data › From File › From Text/CSV
Check Semicolon and choose Do not detect data types
Set the three types with Using Locale and Portuguese (Brazil)
Close & Load, then rename the query Freight
trap: Letting Excel detect the types first means a date may already be read in the wrong order before you name the locale.

prompt: In `WebOrders`, with `Unit price` typed using English (United States), what do the three months add up to as `Qty` times `Unit price`, cancelled orders included, in reais?
hint: Twenty-four rows; September has a price with fifty centavos.

prompt: A student whose Excel is set to English imports the courier's file and leaves Data Type Detection at its default. Which symptom gives the mistake away most plainly?
hint: Read `18,90` the way an English-language computer reads numbers.

choices.text: A freight of 1890 where the file says 18,90
choices.why: Right. The comma is read as a thousands separator, so every freight value is a hundred times too large.

choices.text: Every single row of the table turns into an error
choices.why: Most values convert without complaint, which is the danger: they convert to the wrong thing.

choices.text: The order codes lose the letter W at the start
choices.why: The codes are text and no locale touches them.

choices.text: The weights come out in grams
choices.why: There is no unit conversion; `0,75` becomes 75 for the same reason as the freight.
